REPORT
I. Introduction and Background
1.1 The Commission for Air Quality Management in National Capital Region and Adjoining Areas
Bill, 2021 was introduced in Lok Sabha on July 30, 2021. This Bill provided for the constitution of a
Commission for better co-ordination, research, identification, and resolution of problems related to air
quality in the National Capital Region (NCR) and adjoining areas. Adjoining areas were defined as areas
in Haryana, Punjab, Rajasthan, and Uttar Pradesh, adjoining the National Capital Territory of Delhi and
NCR, where any source of pollution may cause adverse impact on air quality in the NCR. This Bill also
sought to dissolve the Environment Pollution Prevention and Control Authority established in the NCR in
1998. An Ordinance establishing a similar Commission was promulgated in October 2020 which lapsed
in March 2021 and was repromulgated in April 2021. This Bill repealed the 2021 Ordinance.
1.2 The Statement of Object and Reasons, with the Bill, succinctly stated that the Bill aimed to
establish a Commission for Air Quality Management in the National Capital Region (NCR) and its
adjoining areas to address the ongoing air pollution crisis while noting that despite efforts by Committees,
Courts, and ad hoc measures, air quality remains a significant concern in the region. Through the Bill, a
permanent, statutory authority with broad powers to tackle pollution, including controlling stubble
burning, vehicular emissions, industrial pollution, and other sources, through coordination between states
and various stakeholders was sought to be created. It was stated that the Bill will replace previous
temporary Committees and Ordinances, focusing on comprehensive, collaborative actions, and enforce
penalties for violations. The Bill also included sub-committees to support monitoring, enforcement, and
research efforts, ensuring long-term, effective solutions to air pollution.
1.3 The said Bill was passed by Houses of Parliament and notified on 13 thAugust, 2021 as“The
Commission for Air Quality Management in NCR and Adjoining Areas Act, 2021”(CAQM Act
henceforth) (Annexure I) .
1.4 The Commission for Air Quality Management in NCR and Adjoining Areas (Imposition,
Collection and Utilization of Environmental Compensation for Stubble Burning) Rules, 2023 and
subsequent amendments.
1.4.1 India is committed to create a clean environment and pollution free air as mandated in the
Constitution of India. The Committee appointed under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 has taken
measures to deal with the menace of air pollution, particularly in the National Capital Region. By orders
1

passed from time to time, the courts have also set upad hoccommittees to aid and assist them on it
oringand implementation of its orders and generally to take steps to deal with air pollution. Even then,
quality of air in the air shed of the National Capital Region and in the adjoining areas remains a major
cause of concern. There is a need to evolve and implement a consolidated approach for monitoring,
tackling and eliminating the causes for air pollution and identifying, specifying and rigorously enforcing
measures for elimination and mitigation of air pollution, including but not limited to, controlling or
eliminating the activities of stubble burning, vehicular pollution, industrial emissions, road dust, biomass
burning and urban construction. To deal with the problem of Stubble Burning and fulfil the provision of
Section 15 of the Commission for Air Quality Management in NCR and Adjoining Areas Act,2021,The
Commission for Air Quality Management in NCR and Adjoining Areas (Imposition, Collection and
Utilization of Environmental Compensation for Stubble Burning) Rules, 2023were framed and notified.
1.4.2 The Commission for Air Quality Management in NCR and Adjoining Areas(Imposition,
Collection and Utilization of Environmental Compensation for Stubble Burning) Rules, 2023 have been
framed in accordance with the provision in Section 15 of the Commission for Air Quality Management in
National CapitalRegion and Adjoining Areas Act, 2021 which provides that “the Commission may
impose and collect environmental compensation from farmers causing air pollution by stubble burning, at
such rate and in such manner,as maybe prescribed”.
1.4.3Background of imposition of Environmental Compensation:Prior to the enactment of the
CAQM Act, the Hon’ble National Green Tribunal (Principal Bench),
New Delhi through its judgment dated 10.12.2015 in Application No. 118 of 2013 titled as 2.
Vikrant Kumar Tongad Vs. Environment Pollution (Prevention & Control) Authority & Ors.,inter alia,
directed as under:
“In view of the above discussion and the stand taken before us by the different State
Governments and the Ministry, we dispose of this application with the following directions:
XXX
All the States which have issued Notification prohibiting agriculture crop residue burning
shall ensure that the Notifications are enforced rigorously and proper action is taken against the
defaulters. Any person or body that is found offending this direction would be liable to pay
Environmental Compensation as follows:
a.Small land holders having an area less than 2 Acres shall pay Environmental Compensation
of Rs. 2500/- per incidence.
b.Land holders having land area more than 2 Acres but Less than 5 Acres shall pay
Environmental Compensation of Rs. 5000/- per incidence.
2

c.Land holders having land area more than 5 Acres shall pay Environmental Compensation of
Rs. 15000/-per incidence.”
State Governments had been imposing Environmental Compensation on the defaulters by following the
directions of Hon’ble Tribunal in the above-mentioned order.
1.4.4 Statutory Framework for imposition of Environmental Compensation:The Commission for
Air Quality Management in National Capital Region and Adjoining Areas Ordinance, 2020 (No. 13 of
2020) was promulgated on 28.10.2020, for co-ordination, research, identification and resolution of
problems surrounding the air quality in National Capital Region and Adjoining Areas. Upon it’s lapse, the
Commission for Air Quality Management in National Capital Region and Adjoining Areas Ordinance,
2021 (No. 4 of 2021) was promulgated on 13.4.2021, for co-ordination, research, identification and
resolution of problems surrounding the air quality in National Capital Region and Adjoining Areas.
Subsequently, The Commission for Air Quality Management in National Capital Region and Adjoining
Areas Act, 2021 (No. 29 of 2021) was enacted in the Parliament on 13.8.2021.
1.4.5 The Commission for Air Quality Management in National Capital Region and Adjoining Areas
Act, 2021 inter-alia has the following key provisions:
(a) Constitution of the Commission for Air Quality Management in NCR and Adjoining Areas to
perform the functions;
(b) Appointment of Chairperson, Members and Member-Secretary of the Commission
(c) Constitution of the Sub-committees on Monitoring and Identification, Safeguarding and
Enforcement, Research and Development;
(d) Powers and functions of the Commission to take all such measures and issue directions for the
purpose of protection and improvement of air quality in NCR and Adjoining Areas;
(e) Authorisation of any person by the Commission to perform the functions of the Commission;
(f) Commission to provide an effective framework, action plan and appropriate steps for tackling
the problem of stubble burning and monitor the measures taken by the States to prevent stubble
burning, in the NCR and Adjoining Areas;
(g) Penalty for contravention of provisions, rules, orders or directions issued by the Commission;
(h) Imposition and collection of Environmental Compensation from farmers causing air pollution
by stubble burning;
(i) Payment of grants by the Central Government to the Commission for its functioning;
(j) Maintaining accounts by the Commission and conducting audits;
3

(k) Powers of Central Government to make rules to carry out the provisions.
1.4.6 The Commission for Air Quality Management in National Capital Region and Adjoining Areas
(hereinafter referred to as the “Commission”) was constituted on 23.04.2021 in accordance with the
provisions of the Commission for Air Quality Management in National Capital Region and Adjoining
Areas Act, 2021 (hereinafter referred to as the “Act”). Section 14 of the Act provides for penalty for
contravention of provisions of the Act, rules, orders and directions issued by the Commission. Section 14
of the Act,inter alia,stipulates as under:
“(1) Any non-compliance or contravention of any provisions of this Act, rules made there under or any
order or direction issued by the Commission, shall be an offence punishable with imprisonment for a term
which may extend up to five years or with fine which may extend up to one crore rupees or with both:
Provided that the provisions of this section shall not apply to any farmer for causing air pollution
by stubble burning or mismanagement of agricultural residue.”
1.4.7 While Section 14(1) of the Act provides for punishment with imprisonment which may extend
upto five years or with fine which may extend upto one crore or with both for any non-compliance or
contraventions of the Act or rules or directions, the said provision is not applicable to any farmer for
causing air pollution by stubble burning or mismanagement of agricultural residue.
1.4.8 Accordingly, Section 15 of the Act, provides for imposition of Environmental Compensation on
farmers for causing air pollution by stubble burning. Section 15 of the Act,inter alia,stipulates as under:
“The Commission may impose and collect environmental compensation from farmers causing air
pollution by stubble burning, at such rate and in such manner, as may be prescribed.”
1.4.9 Section 25 provides for making rules by the Central Government to carry out the provisions of the
Act. Section 25 of the Act,inter-aliastipulates as under:
“(1) The Central Government may, by notification, make rules to carry out the provisions of this
Act.
(2) In particular and without prejudice to the generality of the foregoing power, such rules may
provide for all or any of the following matters, namely:—
xxxxx
(h) the rate at which, and the manner in which, the environmental compensation shall be
imposed and collected under section 15;”
1.4.10 In view of the provisions of the Act, the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate
Changevideits Notification No. G.S.R. 322(E) dated 28.04.2023 notified the Commission for Air Quality
4

Management in National Capital Region and Adjoining Areas (Imposition, Collection and Utilization of
Environmental Compensation for Stubble Burning) Rules, 2023,(Annexure II) which,inter alia,
stipulates as under:
“Imposition of environmental compensation for stubble burning.—The Commission may
impose and collect environmental compensation on farmers liable for burning stubble, at the
following rates, namely: -
(a) The Farmer having an area of land less than two acres shall pay an environmental
compensation of rupees two thousand five hundred;
(b) The Farmer having an area of land of two acres or more but less than five acres shall
pay an environmental compensation of rupees five thousand;
(c) The Farmers having an area of more than five acres shall pay an environmental
compensation of rupees fifteen thousand.”
1.4.11Amendment in the Extant Provision for implementation of Environmental Compensation:
The Hon’ble Supreme Court vide its Order dated 23.10.2024 in Writ Petition (Civil) No. 13029 of 1985
in the matter of M.C. Mehta Vs. Union of India & Ors.,inter alia, observed and directed as under:
“…The environmental compensation that is stated to be recovered is minimal.
The learned Additional Solicitor General appearing for the Commission states that the
Government of India has exercised power under Section 15 of the Commission for Air
Quality Management in National Capital Region and Adjoining Areas Act, 2021 (for short, "the Act") and
has adopted the formula laid down by the National Green Tribunal for fixing rates of compensation while
framing Rules. Nothing is placed on record to show that the rulemaking power has been exercised in
terms of Section 15 of the Act prescribing the rates of compensation. The importance of Section 15 of the
Act has to be understood in the context of the proviso to sub-section (1) of Section 14 of the Act, which
excludes the farmers from the applicability of penal provisions. When such a concession is given to the
farmers, power has to be exercised by the Government of India under Section 15 of the Act
by framing rules and by providing appropriate Environmental Compensation. The Government cannot
blindly rely upon the formula fixed by the National Green Tribunal.
We direct the Government of India to reconsider the issue and take action under Section
15 of the Act for prescribing proper rates of compensation. Section 15 of the Act talks about the
manner of collecting compensation. Unless proper exercise of power under Section 15 of the Act
is made, there cannot be any effective action against the wrongdoers. We expect the Government
to take actionwithin two weeks from today.”
1.4.12 The Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change, accordinglyvideNotification No.
G.S.R. 690(E) dated 06.11.2024, notified the Commission for Air Quality Management in
National
5

Capital Region and Adjoining Areas (Imposition, Collection and Utilization of Environmental
Compensation for Stubble Burning) Amendment Rules, 2024, (AnnexureIII)inter alia, substituting the
rule 3 as under:
“The Commission may impose environmental compensation as per the provisions of the Act
for stubble burning, at the following rates:-
(a) the Farmer having an area of land of less than two acres shall pay an environmental
compensation of five thousand rupees, per incidence;
(b) the Farmer having an area of land of two acres or more but less than five acres shall
pay an environmental compensation of ten thousand rupees, per incidence;
(c) the Farmer having an area of land of more than five acres shall pay an environmental
compensation of thirty thousand rupees, per incidence.”
Applicability of the CAQM Rules, 2023 is to the States of Punjab, Haryana, Uttar Pradesh, Rajasthan
and NCT of Delhi.
1.5 Keeping in view its significance, the CAQM Rules 2023 was taken up for detailed examination
by the Committee. The Committee had sought information through Background notes and
Questionnaire from the nodal Ministry i.e. Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change for
their comments/clarifications. The subject was deliberated upon by the Committee in its two meetings
held on 3 rd and 18 th December, 2024. During the course of its examination, the Committee had long
ranging discussion with the representatives of the (i) Ministry of Environment, Forests and Climate
Change, Commission for Air Quality Management and Central Pollution Control Board on 3 rd
December, 2024 and (ii) On 18 th December, 2024 with the representatives of the Ministries of
Agriculture & Farmers' Welfare, New and Renewable Energy, Petroleum and Natural Gas, Power,
Commerce and Industry (Department of Promotion of Industry and Internal trade) besides the nodal

process, wherever felt necessary, the Commission has also come up with much stringent emission
standards / norms for various polluting activities in NCR, as compared to the national standards. These
directions are vigorously followed up through periodic progress reviews and issuing records of such
deliberations, supplementary orders, clarifications etc. and numerous official correspondences from time
to time.
5. II EXAMINATION OF RULES, OBSERVATIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS
1. After detailed deliberations amongst the Committee based on inputs from the respective Ministries
namely the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change, Agriculture & Farmers' Welfare, New
and Renewable Energy, Petroleum and Natural Gas, Power and Commerce and Industry (Department of
Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade along with experts on the subject of stubble burning, the
observations/recommendations of the Committee are put forth in the succeeding paragraphs: -
1.1 The Committee, after a bare reading of the rules, is of the view that comprehensive and precise
definitions can be included for terms such as "stubble burning," "environmental compensation," and
"affected areas." As this will help ensure clarity and uniform interpretation across all stakeholders and
legal authorities. Specific definitions will reduce ambiguity and allow for more effective implementation
and enforcement of the rules. It further is of the view that the inclusion of proviso with a clear definition
for "small and marginal farmers" to identify those who are financially vulnerable would help in ensuring
that special provisions and exemptions, if applicable, are tailored to their needs. Provisions could include
financial aid, technology support for stubble management, or reduced penalties for stubble burning in
case of non-compliance, based on the farmer's economic capacity.The Committee observes that by
addressing these key definitions, the rules could be more effective in achieving both environmental
objectives and providing fair treatment to all farmers, especially the economically disadvantaged.
1.2 The Committee observes that to safeguard the rights and interests of farmers and ensure the
prevention of unjust penalization for stubble burning, it is essential to establish a robust redressal
mechanism. This mechanism shall provide a clearly defined process for addressing grievances related to
erroneous or disputed challans. It must include the designation of the competent appellate authority,
18

stipulate a prescribed timeline for resolution, and outline the procedural framework for adjudication.
Such a system will enable farmers to challenge wrongful actions effectively and uphold principles of
fairness and accountability. In this context, t he Committee notes that Rule 4 which concerns
“Collection of Environmental Compensation for stubble burning” and outlines theprocedures for
the Collection of Environmental Compensation for Stubble Burning, exhibits certain ambiguities
regarding the delineation of roles, responsibilities, and accountability mechanisms. Sub-clause (3) of
Rule 4 states that if the Farmer fails to pay the challan amount within the period specified under sub-
rule(2),the Commission shall prepare a certificate specifying the amount due from the Farmer and
forward the certificate along with the form of challan to the officer authorised by the respective State
Government or, Union territory, as the case may be, in this regard. The Committee observes that the
term "officer" is vague and this lack of specificity might cause delays or confusion in implementation as
responsibilities could be unclear. The rule should specify the officer's designation, e.g., "Tehsildar,"
"Sub-Divisional Magistrate (SDM)," or "Revenue Officer" responsible for land revenue collection in the
respective region or the state pollution control board or the authority managing the penalties collected
from stubble burning.The Committee, in this regard, recommends that suitable and appropriate
modifications may be carried out in (i) designating an authority who will be able to address the
grievances of farmers in a time bound manner, (ii) clarityon the term “officer” for issuing
challans.
1.3 The Committee notes that i n Sub Rule (4) of Rule 4 it has been stated that“the
officer referred to in sub rule (4) shall on receipt of the certificate and the form of challan,
shall proceed to recover the amount specified there under from the farmer as if it were an
arrear of the landrevenue. “TheCommittee notes that the error in the wording, which was
typographical, has been rectified and substituted by “sub rule (3)”. The Committee further
notes that Sub-clause (3) of Rule 4 specifies that a Certificate will be prepared, but there is no
prescribed format annexed, leading to variability in implementation. The Committee is of the view
that absence of a standardized Certificate Form could lead to inconsistencies and legal ambiguities.
Therefore, the Committee recommends that a standardised Certificate Form be prepared on the
lines of Challan and put in Annexure of the Rules.
1.4 The Committee notes that Sub-clause (5) of Rule 4 states that“The officer of the respective State
Government or, Union territory who maintains the land revenue record as prevalent in the respective
State Government or, Union territory shall ensure that such record is marked with red entry against the
Farmer where from the incident of stubble burning is found or reported to burn stubble or there is a
proof to the effect that stubble burning has happened in the land;”The Committee deduces that, as per
provision of the Rule, t he “RED ENTRY” shall be maintained by the designated authority in the
respective State Government or Union Territory and this entry shall serve as a record of non-
19

compliance with the regulations prohibiting stubble burning and may be considered for future
regulatory actions or incentives. Noting this, the Committee observes that the rules does not specify
with clarity that whether “RED ENTRY” is to be marked for thefarmers who had paid the fine, or
not paid the fine or for all the cases where stubble is burned or reported for maintaining the records.
Also, it is not made clear,which authority will maintain these records of “RED ENTRY”.
Therefore, it is necessary to enhance the clarity of the provisions. The Committee feels that the
officer of the respective State Government or Union Territory who maintains the land revenue
record, as prevalent in the respective State Government or Union Territory, should ensure that such
record is marked with a red entry against the farmer’s land parcel where stubble burning hasbeen
detected or reported; or a fine has been imposed for stubble burning, regardless of whether it has
been paid or not; or any other evidence of stubble burning exists. The Committee, therefore
recommends that, the Ministry may examine the suitable provisions in this regard and make
necessary amendments or issue necessary clarifications/ instructions for bringing clarity.
1.4.1 The Committee further observes that incorporating an exit provision or removal mechanism for
the Red Entry under the Rule would significantly help farmers affected by such entries. A structured
approach could include a time-bound removal mechanism, where the Red Entry is automatically erased
after a specified period if no repeat offense occurs. Additionally, farmers could be provided an
opportunity to remove the entry by adopting eco-friendly practices, providing proof of compliance, and
attending awareness programs on stubble management. Also, to ensure fairness, an appeal and review
process can be established, allowing farmers to contest a Red Entry by submitting counter-evidence
before a designated authority and if an entry is found to be erroneous or based on incorrect reports, it
could be removed immediately upon verification.Based on these observations, the Committee
recommends introducing an incentive-based Red entry removal system, enabling early removal for
farmers actively participating in sustainable farming practices or government-supported stubble
management programs.The Committee is of the firm view that these measures would help promote
justice and fairness, prevent undue harassment, encourage positive behavioral change over punitive
measures, and strike a balance between environmental concerns and the socio-economic realities of
farmers.
1.5 The Committee notes that the Sub-clause (6)of Rule 4 states that “The environmental
compensation collected under this rule shall be deposited in the account of respective State
Pollution Control Board or Pollution Control Committee.”This, the Committee understands means
that the environmental compensation collected under this rule shall be deposited to a Stubble
Management Fund managed by a particular authority to use this fund for better management of
20

crop residue in the respective states or regions. However, the Committee observes that this sub-
clause (6), lack explicit provisions governing the utilization of environmental compensation
funds and thus it is imperative to specify the purposes for fund allocation, designate the
authorities authorized to approve disbursements, and establish mechanisms for monitoring
and ensuring effective utilization as incorporating such provisions will enhance transparency
and accountability in fund management.
1.6 Drawing on its observations in above para, the Committee is of the view that while the
current Rules outline the framework for imposing and collecting environmental compensation,
they lack specific provisions regarding its utilization. Thus, the Committee feels that an
appropriate addition of a new Rule will help in aligning the same with their stated purpose of
Imposition, Collection, and Utilization of Environmental Compensation for Stubble Burning.
I n v i e w o f t h e f o r e g o i n g t h e C o m m i t t e e r e c o m m e n d s t h a t a n e w
s u b - r u l e r e l a t i n g t o u tilization of Environmental Compensation Fund for stubble
burning be incorporated in the Rules so that the Environmental Compensation Funds get
utilized to promote sustainable agriculture practices by subsidizing residue management
technologies, incentivizing crop diversification, supporting biomass utilization
infrastructure, research in the area of crop residue management and educating farmers one
co-friendly practices, etc. to reduce stubble burning for sustainable farming. Further the
respective State Governments, in consultation with the Commission, may be authorized to
formulate and issue appropriate guidelines and notifications for the implementation of
incentivization measures as deemed necessary.
1.7 The Committee consciously notes that its mandate is to explicitly examine the Commission for
Air Quality Management in National Capital Region and Adjoining Areas (Imposition, Collection and
Utilization of Environmental Compensation for Stubble Burning) Rules, 2023. However, based on
ground insights, comments from representatives of various Ministries and other experts including
concerns raised by the Hon’ble Members of the Committee,the Committee outlines the following further
recommendations/ observations/ suggestions for consideration of the Ministry/ relevant stakeholders:
(i) The Committee recommends towards establishing a mechanism by State Governments, in
consultation with the Commission to determine and benchmark a minimum price for paddy crop
residue. This price should function similarly to a Minimum Support Price (MSP) to provide
farmers with guaranteed returns upon selling their stubble. These benchmark price can be
reviewed and notified annually before the Kharif harvest season, ensuring they reflect farmers'
costs for residue collection, including labour and machinery.
21

(ii)The Committee is of the view that establishing a Real-time Mapping of Crop Acreage and
Forecasting of Crop Maturity and Weather System to estimate the land under cultivation for different
crops and their yields to assess the total district-wise crop yield and Real-time forecasting of crop
maturity and weather for better planning and efficacy of technological and human resources to manage
harvesting and crop residue management timely and efficiently will go a long way in addressing the issue
of stubble burning.The Committee therefore recommends the establishment of Real-time Mapping
of Crop Acreage and Forecasting of Crop Maturity and Weather system.
(iii) Based on the inputs received and noting the initiatives being taken and noting that transport
costs are one of the main constraints in the transportation of residues,the Committee is of the view that
establishing interim storage facilities in different districts for collecting crop residue in areas where
industries or end users are unavailable within 20-50 km., would facilitate t he local
aggregators/agribusiness to enable the collection of crop residue/bail efficiently and timely besides
motivating local entrepreneurs and aggregators to facilitate CRM.
(iv) The Committee notes that a primary concern is the limited window of about 25 days available to
farmers between the harvesting of paddy and the sowing of the next crop. The Committee believes that
this short window between the Rabi and Kharif crops is one of the main reasons why farmers resort to
stubble burning.Therefore, the Committee recommends that the respective State Governments
incentivize the adoption of short-duration paddy varieties as an alternative to long-duration
varieties such as PUSA 44. This can include measures such as standardizing procurement
processes, enforcing seed certification bans, and providing financial support to farmers who opt
for crop diversification under government schemes.The procurement guidelines of the Food
Corporation of India (FCI) for rice should align with the quality standards of short-duration paddy
varieties.The Committee further recommends that the Union Government assess and implement
an impact evaluation framework for ongoing crop diversification incentives under schemes like
the Crop Diversification Plan, ensuring the scalability of these incentives to other states.
(v) The Committee is of the considered opinion, after hearing representatives of various Ministries
there is a need to integrate agriculture residue into bio energy generation effectively.Towards this the
Committee recommends the formulation of a Unified National Policy for the integration of
agriculture residue into bio energy generation. This policy should ensure inter-ministerial
coordination across Agriculture, New and Renewable Energy, Petroleum and Natural Gas,
Industry, Health, and Environment Ministries, and prioritize the adoption of technologies like bio
ethanol, compressed biogas, and biomass pellets. It should address ex-situ costs for crop residue
management, provide financial incentives, develop supply chain infrastructure, and implement
awareness programs for farmers, ensuring both economic viability and environmental
sustainability.
22

(vi) During the deliberations on the issue, the Committee noted that Ministry of Health & Family
Welfare is neither a part of the Inter Ministerial Committee constituted on the issue of stubble burning
and also not represented in the Commission for Air Quality Management (CAQM). The Committee
noted that the Air Pollution and worsening air quality poses serious health risks for millions of residents
of Delhi and NCR.Therefore, the Committee recommends that representatives of Ministry of
Health & Family Welfare at various forums in connection with Air Pollution and stubble burning
related issues may be ensured.
(vii)The Committee also recommends that the Ministry of Environment, Forests and Climate
Change, should undertake periodic reviews, based on stakeholder feedback and evolving
environmental conditions, to ensure continuous improvement and adaptability of the notified Rules.

to make su bmissions on the subje ct. Thereafter , the Chairman of the Co mmittee requested
there p resentatives of th e Ministry and both the exp erts to make their su bmissions, in
brief, one by one on this issue.
3. The Joint Secretary of the Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers’Welfare in her
submissions informed the Committee that she was dealing with farm mechanization in
Ministry of Agriculture under which they are providing all kinds of machinery to the
farmers on subsidized basis. On the issue of Air pollution, the Ministry has started a
scheme called ‘Crop Residue Management Schemer 2018 with their three folds of
interventions. One is providing machines for managing the paddy straw that is generated
in the fields, and, for that they are giving subsidy at the rate of 50% to the farmers, and for
establishing Custom Hiring Centres, provided 80% subsidy, through which the farmers
can rent- out machines and use it form an aging the paddy straw.
3.1 The Ministry has further stated that the second intervention is for providing project-
based support for ex-situ management of the paddy straw under which they have provided
65% of the cost of the machine to the farmers for purchasing of machines; 25% the
industry pitches in; and10%, the aggregators gives as a beneficiary. So under this, the
paddy straw is collect and as a supply chain, it is provided to the industry which is using
it. The third component of the Scheme is that they are doing aggressive campaigning and
promotion and carry out the Information, Education& Communication (IEC) campaign
through Indian Council for Agricultural Research (ICAR) Institutes, and through the State
governments, to make an informed suggestion to the farmers not to burn the paddy straw
and how it is having an ill-effect and how, by not burning the paddy straw, they could be
net and have the nutrients back in the soil and also have a remunerative income.
4. The Joint Secretary, Ministry of Power stated that they have introduced a policy in
the year 2017 for co-firing of biomass pellets in their thermal power plants. The Ministry
has already created a dedicated Mission called ‘SAMARTH Mission’ under which they
are focusing that the thermal power plants should co-fire biomass-based pellets along with
coal. The Ministry is promoting creation of biomass chain and creation of pellet-
manufacturing chain through the above Mission. The Ministry has further stated that they
34

are helping their thermal power plants to actually migrate, at least, up to 5 to 10 per cent
and they have targeted that there should be 5 per cent on co-firing and the same will be
raised to 7 per cent in subsequent years. The Ministry has further informed the Committee
that they are focusing primarily across the country and also in the National Capital Region
(NCR).
5. The representative of the Ministry of New and Renewable Energy informed that
they are running a Scheme, namely, the Bio Energy Programme, under which there are
three components - Waste to Energy, Biomass Programme and Biogas Programme.
Biomass comes from various resources including stubble, that is being used for
manufacturing of briquette and pellet manufacturing and they are providing subsidy for
the purpose. In addition to that, the biomass is also going for co-generation and
compressed biogas production and converted into biogas. The Committee was also
apprised that so far, they have 15.31 lakh tones per year consumption of biomass in three
States from these commissioned projects.
6. The Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas apprised the Committee that they have a
policy called SATAT in which they manufacture Compressed Biogas(CBG) and as of
now, in the NCR Region, two plants are commissioned with capacity of 21 tonnes per day
and one plant is under construction with a capacity of 15 tonnes per day. For effective
collection of the biomass, they have started a Scheme this year called BAM, i.e., Biomass
Aggregation Machinery The Ministry is providing 50 per cent incentive to the CBG
producers for purchase of the biomass set under this Scheme. For effective evacuation of
the gas that i s produced, they have a scheme for pipeline infrastructure under which they
have provided Rs50lakhs per kilometer for laying down the pipeline, which connect a
CBG producer to a CBG entity.
7. The Ministry of Commerce and Industry in their presentation stated that they should
find ways in which parali or stubble can be used as an alternative fuel for cement kilns and
how it can be used by paper industry and the particle boards made by them can be used
for furniture industry. The Ministry has further stated that they will soon have stakeholder
consultation with furniture industry and particle board manufacturers to understand what
the requirement of furniture industry is because they have been told that parali has lot of
silica content which makes it little difficult for equipments to manufacture furniture as
well as make good paper out of it.
7.1 The Ministry has further stated that they have requested their two National level
Institutes, the Central Paper and Pulp Research Institute (CPPRI) and National Council for
Cement and Building Material to do research as to how this stubble can be used as an
alternative fuel or feed stock for paper manufacturing.
8. The Special Secretary& Chairman, CPCB in his presentation, inter alia, informed
the Committee that in the earlier meeting with the Commission for Air Quality
Management in NCR and Adjoining areas on Dec 3, 2024 a detailed presentation was
made by the Chairperson of CAQM on their role. Under the regulatory framework, thereis
an Act in place known as the Commission for Air Quality management in NCR and
Adjoining Areas Act which came into force in 2021.
35

8.1 The Ministry apprised the Committee that under the Act the powers have been
vested with the Commission for issuing directions and it does monitoring exercise and
reform exercise in consultation with all the State Governments; the State Governments of
Punjab, Haryana, Delhi, Rajasthan and some parts of Uttar Pradesh and respective State
Pollution Control Boards. Under that umbrella, the CAQM holds meetings and issues
directions from time to time for improvement of air quality. They categorized the sources
of air pollution in Delhi and NCR as below - (i) dust, that is, dust from consistent
demolition waste as also the road dust, (ii) vehicular pollution, (iii) industrial
pollution,(iv)the pollution from burning of biomass and waste, and (v) the episodic events,
which happen in the months of October and November, when stubble burning and fire
crackers etc. contribute to the air pollution. To control that the Commission has issued a
number of directions and the Ministry has also come out with Rules.
8.2 Further, the Ministry apprised the Committee that imposition of fines, etc., is also a
component of the overall stubble burning management framework and
monitoring exercise is done by the CAQM with support of the scientists from CPCB and
also deputed core scientists by the Ministry and CAQM. The AirQuality Index is measured
by the continuous ambient air quality monitoring stations which have been put up in Delhi
and other parts of the Country.
9. Dr. Abhishek Kar in his brief presentation on the subject apprised the Committee
regarding CAQM Rules, the insights from the field, those are all based out of their
research, which is peer reviewed. Firstly, it is the problem of crop residue burning and
they did a survey of about 1,500 farmers to understand the problem on the ground. One of
the issues is partial burning which farmers often resorted to. He has further informed the
Committee about the CRM Machines. Farmers are just adopting the machines not the
package of farming practices.
9.1 He has submitted before the Committee that combine harvesters should be fitted
with Super Straw Management System and then farmers should use the machine.
Unfortunately, farmers are not doing that. They are directly using the super seeder. This
sometimes is raising complaints around pesticides, etc. so that this is in-situ approach. Next
is ex situ approach. One challenge that they have seen is in terms of contract enforcement.
Often farmers are told that their harvest is going to be picked up, but often it is not getting
picked up. On the other hand, sometimes it so happens that after the baling machines are
used, the material is kept there and there is a delay in picking that up. In winters, the
quality of straw is getting damaged. There is a delay between harvesting and bringing it to
the industry. He highlighted that the short duration seed variety is getting more popular
yet evidence on the ground suggest that it is coming as broken. He suggest that while there
is a complete ban on burning of stubble, one has to differentiate between partial burning
and complete burning.
10. Dr. Suresh Jain in his submission before the Committee stated that there is a
mismatch between what we see in the field and how policies or strategies are implemented
in the case of stubble burning. He has further mentioned about the number of subsidies
given to equipments and supply chain. The Companies, which can support the amount of
36

stubble which is getting generated in those areas, are less in number and other aspects
comes like, weather, crop maturity, depending upon the variety of growing paddy and
infrastructural resources required.
10.1 He has further suggested for a real-time forecasting system with integrated
parameters of size of crop acreage, hot-spot in terms of where more burning occurs and
how the weather is going to be there can help in making accurate forecasts about location,
type of meteorology, rainfall patterns, allowing for collection of resources in a better way
with the minimum available time.

MINISTRY OF ENVIRONMENT, FOREST AND CLIMATE CHANGE
NOTIFICATION
New Delhi, the 28th April, 2023
G.S.R. 322(E).—In exercise of the powers conferred by clause (h) of sub-section (2) of section 25 of the
Commission for Air Quality Management in National Capital Region and Adjoining Areas Act, 2021 (29 of 2021),
the Central Government hereby makes the following rules, namely:-
1. Short title and commencement.—(1) These rules may be called the Commission for Air Quality Management in
National Capital Region and Adjoining Areas (Imposition, Collection and Utilization of Environmental
Compensation for Stubble Burning) Rules, 2023.
(2) They shall apply to the National Capital territory of Delhi, State of Punjab, State of Haryana and National
Capital Region of Rajasthan and Uttar Pradesh.
(3) They shall come into force on the date of their publication in the Official Gazette.
2. Definitions.—(1) In these rules, unless the context otherwise requires, -
(a)“Act” means the Commission for Air Quality Management in National Capital Region and Adjoining Areas
Act, 2021 (29 of 2021);
(b)“Commission” means the Commission for Air Quality Management in National Capital Region and
adjoining areas constituted under section 3;
(c)“Farmer” means the owner or occupier or cultivator of the farming or agricultural land;
(d)“Section” means a section of the Act.
(2) Words and expressions used herein and not defined but defined in the Act shall have the same meanings as
assigned to them in the Act.

4 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : EXTRAORDINARY [P ART II—S EC. 3(i)]
3. Imposition of environmental compensation for stubble burning.—The Commission may impose and collect
environmental compensation on farmers liable for burning stubble, at the following rates, namely:-
(a) The Farmer having an area of land less than two acres shall pay an environmental compensation of rupees
two thousand five hundred;
(b) The Farmer having an area of land of two acres or more but less than five acres shall pay an environmental
compensation of rupees five thousand;
(c) The Farmers having an area of more than five acres shall pay an environmental compensation of rupees
fifteen thousand.
4. Collection of Environmental Compensation for stubble burning.—(1) The environmental compensation
shall be collected from the Farmer in the form of challan as specified in Form annexed to these rules;
(2) The Farmer shall pay the amount in pursuance of challan under these rules within a period not exceeding thirty
days from the date of issuance of form of challan;
(3) If the Farmer fails to pay the challan amount within the period specified under sub-rule (2), the Commission
shall prepare a certificate specifying the amount due from the Farmer and forward the certificate along with
the form of challan to the officer authorised by the respective State Government or, Union territory, as the
case may be, in this regard;
(4) The officer referred to in sub-rule (4) shall, on receipt of the certificate and the form of challan, shall proceed
to recover the amount specified thereunder from the Farmer as if it were an arrear of the land revenue;
(5) The officer of the respective State Government or, Union territory who maintains the land revenue record as
prevalent in the respective State Government or, Union territory shall ensure that such record is marked with
red entry against the Farmer where from the incident of stubble burning is found or reported to burn stubble
or there is a proof to the effect that stubble burning has happened in the land;
(6) The environmental compensation collected under this rule shall be deposited in the account of respective State
Pollution Control Board or Pollution Control Committee.
[F. No. Q-15014/10/2021-CPA]

MINISTRY OF ENVIRONMENT, FOREST AND CLIMATE CHANGE
NOTIFICATION
New Delhi, the 6th November, 2024
G.S.R. 690(E).—In exercise of the powers conferred by clause (h) of sub-section (2) of section 25 of the
Commission for Air Quality Management in National Capital Region and Adjoining Areas Act, 2021 (29 of 2021), the
Central Government hereby makes the following rules to amend the Commission for Air Quality Management in
National Capital Region and Adjoining Areas (Imposition, Collection and Utilization of Environmental Compensation
for Stubble Burning) Rules, 2023, namely:-
1. Short title and commencement.- (1) These rules may be called the Commission for Air Quality Management in
National Capital Region and Adjoining Areas (Imposition, Collection and Utilization of Environmental Compensation
for Stubble Burning) Amendment Rules, 2024.
(2) They shall come into force on the date of their publication in the Official Gazette.
2.In the Commission for Air Quality Management in National Capital Region and Adjoining Areas (Imposition,
Collection and Utilization of Environmental Compensation for Stubble Burning) Rules, 2023 (hereinafter referred to as
the said rules), for rule 3, the following rule shall be substituted, namely:-
“3.The Commission may impose environmental compensation as per the provisions of the Act for stubble
burning, at the following rates:-
(a) the Farmer having an area of land of less than two acres shall pay an environmental compensation of five
thousand rupees, per incidence;

compensation of ten thousand rupees, per incidence;
(c) the Farmer having an area of land of more than five acres shall pay an environmental compensation of
thirty thousand rupees, per incidence.”.
3.In the said rules, in sub-rule (4) of rule 4, for the bracket, words and figures “The officer referred to in sub-rule
(4)”, the bracket, words and figures “The officer referred to in sub-rule (3)” shall be substituted.

CHAPTER II
COMMISSION FOR AIR QUALITY MANAGEMENT IN NATIONAL CAPITAL REGION AND
ADJOINING AREAS
3.(1) The Central Government shall, by notification in the Official Gazette, constitute
a body to be known as the Commission for Air Quality Management in National Capital
Region and Adjoining Areas to exercise the powers conferred upon, and to perform the
functions assigned to, that Commission under this Act.
(2) The Commission shall consist of the following Members, namely:––
(a) a full-time Chairperson having experience of not less than fifteen years in the
field of environment protection and pollution control or having administrative
experience of not less than twenty-five years;
(b) a representative of the Secretary to the Government of India in the Ministry
of Environment, Forest and Climate Change, who shall be an officer not below the rank
of Joint Secretary,ex officio;
(c) fiveex officioMembers who are either Chief Secretaries, or Secretaries
in-charge of the department dealing with environment protection in the National Capital
Territory of Delhi and the States of Punjab, Haryana, Rajasthan and Uttar Pradesh;
(d) one full-time Member who is or has been a Joint Secretary to the Government
of India;
(e) three full-time independent technical Members to be appointed from amongst
persons having specific knowledge and experience in matters relating to air pollution;
(f) one technical Member from the Central Pollution Control Board,ex officio;
(g) one technical Member to be nominated by the Indian Space Research
Organisation,ex officio;

(2) The Central Government may remove the Chairperson or any Member, other than

(a) is adjudged an insolvent;
(b) engages during his term of office in any paid employment outside the duties

(c) is of unsound mind and stands so declared by a competent court;
(d) has so abused his position as to render his continuance in office prejudicial
to the public interest;
(e) has acquired such financial or other interest as is likely to affect prejudicially
his functions; or

opinion of the Central Government involves moral turpitude:

opportunity of being heard.

leave or otherwise, such one of the Members as the Central Government may, by notification,
authorise in this behalf, shall discharge the functions of the Chairperson until the date on

1. Background 
1.1 The Telecommunications Bill, 2023, aim ed to modernize and consolidate the legal 
framework governing India's telecom sector, recognizing its vital role in economic 
development, digital inclusion, and national security. Its Statement of Objects and Reasons 
(SOR) mentioned that the then current reg ulatory system, based on outdated laws, was no 
longer adequate due to rapid technological advancements.  This Bill propose d a 
comprehensive framework covering authorization of telecom services and networks, spectrum 
assignment etc. and also addresse d national security, public safety, dispute resolution, and 
regulatory compliance. Additionally, it repeal ed the outdated laws, owing to huge technical 
advancements in the telecom sector and technologies, made requisite amendments  to the 
TRAI Act, and retained certain provisions related to power transmission lines. The legislation 
aimed to ensure secure, inclusive, and forward -looking growth of the telecommunications 
sector. 
1.2 The said Bill was introduced in the Lok Sabha on 18 th December, 2023 and was 
passed by Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha on 20 th and 21 st December, 2023. The 
Telecommunications Act, 2023, received the assent of President  of India on December  24, 
2023 and was published in the Official Gazette on the same day  i.e. December 24, 2023. The 
Telecommunication Act 2023 aim ed to amend and consolidate the law relating to 
development, expansion and operation of telecommunication services and telecommunication 
networks, assignment of spectrum, and matters connected therewith. The Telecommunication 
Act 2023 also sought to repeal older legislative framework like Indian Telegraph Act 1885 
and Indian Wireless Telegraph Act 1933 .Guided by the principles of Samavesh (Inclusion), 
Suraksha (Security), Vriddhi (Growth), and Tvarit (Responsiveness), the Act a ims to achieve 
the vision of Viksit Bharat (Developed India). 
1.3 Telecommunications (Telecom Cyber Security) Rules, 2024: One of the objects of 
Statement of Reasons of the Telecommunications Act, 2023 mentions "Provisions for national 
security, public emergency and public safety". In line with this objective, section 22 (1) of the 
Telecommunications Act states that: 
"The Central Government may by rules provide for the measures 
to protect and ensure  cyber security of Telecommunication 
networks and telecommunication services." 
 
1 
 
 
 

Further, section 22(2) Telecommunications Act states that: 
The measures may include collection, analysis and dissemination 
of traffic data that is generated, transmitted, received or stored in 
telecommunication networks. 
Explanation. -For the purposes of this sub -section, the expression 
"traffic data" means any data generated, transmitted, received or 
stored in telecommunication networks including data relating to 
the type, routing, duration or time of a telecommunication. 
 
Accordingly, the  Telecommunications (Telecom Cyber Security) Rules, 2024have been 
notified on 2 1.11.2024. These rules cover the subjects mentioned under the Act.  As ·per the 
allocation of business rules dated 27.09.2024, matters relating to security of telecom networks 
has been allotted to Department of Telecommunications (DoT). 
1.3.1 It goes without saying that Telecommunications play a vital role in delivery of  digital 
services by providing the infrastructure that allows people to connect, communicate, and 
participate in the digital economy. Telecommunications Network and telecommunications 
services are integral to digital inclusion and  for promoting ease of living to the citizens. Thus, 
maintaining integrity and continuity of operation of Telecommunications Network and 
telecommunications services are of paramount importance. For this, it is imperative to adopt 
high standard of  security so that  seamless services of telecommunications may be ensured. 
Safeguarding the citizens by identification of misuse of telecommunications resources is 
highly required. Also, Telecommunications generate hug e-volume of traffic data. Adoption 
of policies and nece ssary data analytics capabilities is required to adopt the measures to 
protect and ensure telecom cyber security. Thus, the objective of these rules  
(Telecommunications (Telecom CyberSecurity) Rules, 2024) is to have an approach for cyber 
security of telecommunication networks and telecommunication services which includes 
tools, policies, security concepts, security safeguards, guidelines, risk management 
approaches, actions, assurance and technologies that can be used to safeguard 
telecommunication networks and telecommunication services against relevant security risks in 
the cyber environment. 
 
1.3.2 The rules are applicable on the telecommunication entities providing 
telecommunication services, or establishing, operating, maintaining, or expanding 
telecommunication network or a  person exempted from the requirement  of authorisation.  
These rules are also applicable to the users involved in misuse of telecommunications 
resources for fraud, cheating, personation and transmitting any message which is fraudulent. 
 
2

1.3.4 Department of Telecom , submits that t he enforcement of the said rules shall  ensure

1.4 Telecommunications (Critical Telecommunication Infrastructure) Rules, 
2024: One of the objects of Statement of Reasons of the Telecommunications Act, 2023 
mentions "Provisions for national security, public  emergency and public  safety". In line  
with this  objective, section 22 (3) of the Act facilitates identification of Critical 
Telecommunication Infrastructure (CTI), disruption o f which shall have debilitating 
impact on national security, economy, public health or safety.  Section 22(4)of the 
Telecommunications Act 2023 says that: 
"The Central Government may by rules provide for the standards, 
security practices, upgradation requirements and procedures to be 
implemented for such Critical Telecommunication Infrastructure." 
Accordingly, the Telecommunications (Critical Telecommunication Infrastructure) Rules, 
2024 have been notified on 22.11.2024. These rules cover the  subjects mentioned under 
the Act. 
 
1.4.1 At present, National Critical Information Infrastructure Protection Center (NCIIPC) is 
an agency notified vide Information Technology (National Critical Information 
I n f r a s t r u c t u r e Protection Center and Manner of Performing Functions and Duties) 
Rules, 2013 on 16.01.2014 under  Section 70A of the Information Technology Act 2000. 
Section 70A of IT Act mentions "The national nodal agency designated under sub-section (]) 
shall be responsible for  all measures including Research and   Development  relating to 
protection of Critical Information Infrastructure." 
 
The key functions  of NCIIPC include identification  and designation of  critical 
information infrastructures (CII) and protect them from specific threats and 
vulnerabilities. Telecom sector has been  declared as critical sector by NCIIPC which has 
declared certain telecom network elements as "protected systems". 
 
1.4.2 The objective of these rules is  to have  a focused monitoring  of standards and 
practices being followed for the Critical equipment in Telecom Sector by various Service 
providers. Service Providers through these rules are obligated to put special focus on their 
"Critical Telecom Equipment" regarding threats, vulnerabilities, risks and cyber 
incidents. The rules are applicable on the telecommunication ent ities whose 
telecommunication network  or part thereof is  declared as  Critical Telecommunication 
Infrastructure (CTI) by Department of Telecom. All licensees - fixed line  and mobile 
operators, internet service providers and other telecom  service providers fall under the 
purview of these CTI rules. 
 
4 

1.4.3 The Department of Telecom has submitted that t he rules have undergone public 
consultation and inputs from several telecom industry  bodies like  STL (Sterlite 
Technologies Pvt. Ltd), ACTO (Association of  Competitive Telecom Operators), BIF  
(Broadband India Forum),  Access Now,  Airtel, Cyril  Amarchand Mangaldas, RJIL  
(Reliance Jio Infocomm Limted), DSCI (Data Security Council of India), TCL (Tata 
Communications Limited), SFLC  (Software Freedom Law  Center) and ITI (Indian 
Telephone Industries) which have been duly considered  before notification of the rules.  
Hence no impediment for implementation of the rules are noticed  and envisaged other 
than the preparatory work which DOT has to undertake for declaration of Critical 
Telecommunication Infrastructure. 
 
1.4.4 It has further been stated that the rules have been framed keeping in view of the 
recent increased requirements of protecting the critical infrastructure in telecom sector 
from increasing cyber threats and to have better monitoring and threat incident response. 
The modification in these rules is not envisaged at present and can be taken care of once 
the situation demands under the provisions of the Telecommunication Act, 2023. 
1.4.5 Thus, the Department of Telcom has informed that the enforcement of these rules will 
strengthen cybersecurity for Critical Telecommunication Infrastructure (CTI) and support the 
broader objective of safeguarding this vital sector against targeted and widespread cyber -
attacks. These rules will play a crucial role in protecting sensitive data from theft and damage.  
With increasing digitalization, data such as personal information, financial rec ords, and 
intellectual property has become immensely valuable. The enforcement of these rules will 
help protect such sensitive data from unauthorized access and theft, while a lso upholding 
personal privacy. In an era where personal information is routinely collected, stored, and 
shared in digital formats, cybersecurity is essential to preserve privacy rights. Safeguarding 
personal data from unauthorized access, surveillance, an d misuse, fosters trust in digital 
services. Furthermore, these measures will help prevent financial losses, assist service 
providers in meeting compliance and legal obligations, and ensure business continuity. Cyber-
attacks on CTI can cause severe disrupt ions, including revenue loss, reputational damage, and 
in some cases, the complete shutdown of operations. Enforcing cybersecurity rules will help 
prevent or mitigate such impacts, thereby supporting uninterrupted business operations. 
 2. The Committee on Subordinate Legislation decided to examine the 
Telecommunications (Critical Telecommunication Infrastructure) Rules, 2024  and the 
Telecommunications (Telecom Cyber Security) Rules, 2024  due to their far -reaching 
implications for national security, privacy,  and the functioning of India’s digital 
infrastructure.  
5 

The Committee deemed it essential to ensure that the delegated legislation remains within the 
permissible limits of the parent Act, adheres to principles of transparency and accountability, 
and does not confer excessive or unchecked powers on the executive. While examining these 
Rules, the Committee has aimed at assessing the potential impact on stakeholders and 
ensuring consistency with constitutional and legal safeguards. During its examination of these 
two Rules, the Committee held three meetings on 4 th February, 2025, 11 th and 25 th March, 
2025.  In these meetings the Committee held detailed deliberations and heard the views and 
submissions of the Secretary and concerned Officers of the Department of Telecom, Ministry 
of Communications, Representatives of the Telecommunication Engineering Centre (TEC) 
and National Centre for Communication Security (NCCS), representatives of Cellular 
Operators Association of India (COAI), T elecom Equipment Manufacturers Association of 
India (TEMA), Bharat Sanchar Nigam Limited (BSNL) and Mahanagar Telephone Nigam 
Limited (MTNL). The Committee also sought information through Questionnaires from the 
Ministry and other organizations. The following paras summarize the views, submissions and 
the deliberations in these meetings and the information shared with the Committee.  
 
2.1 In their submissions before the Committee, Secretary, Department of 
Telecommunications and other Officers mentioned that  these Rules form the backbone of 
cyber telecom security and the world over, telecom has become the basic platform for 
providing any service, innovation, economic development, security or defence and   it is 
incumbent upon the Government and the private sector to ensure  that both the players play 
their respective roles to ensure that adversaries do not gain control of these networks. It was 
submitted that recently, the Government, reco gnizing the importance of cyber security, 
modified the Allocation of Business Rules into  three parts where the original cyber security 
remained with the Ministry of Electronics and Infor mation Technology and the cyber security 
of telecom networks was specifically allocated to Department of Telecom and prosecution 
and punishment on cybercrimes to the Ministry of Home Affairs. With the aid of power point 
presentation, various aspects of the CTI Rules, 2024 were explained and it was also informed 
that that there were no telecom sector specific rules for critical infrastructure that were in 
existence earlier and rules under the IT Act of 2000 were governing them.   The difference 
from the existing rules is that they are more specific to telecom sector and more 
comprehensive and cover the security standards and upgradation processes of telecom 
infrastructure which is declared as critical. This ensures better monitoring of cyber security 
incidents that take place in telecom infrastructure and mitigation measures taken timely.   
Further Rules have been framed under Section 22(4) of the Telecommunications Act which 
provides for standards, security practices, upgradation requirements and procedures to be 
implemented for the critical telecom infrastructure and two organisations in the DoT will  
6 

 
specify the standards, namely, the Telecommunication Engineering Centre (TEC) and the 
National Centre for Communication Security (NCCS), Bangalore.  
2.2 On the Telecom Cyber Security Rules, 2024, it was stated that there are two important 
stakeholders on which these Rules are applicable, viz  the telecommunication entities which 
provide telecommunication services or networks, and the users, who are involved in misuse of 
telecommunication resources for fraud, cheating, etc.   It was submitted that before these rules 
were published, the Ministry went through an extensive round of public consultation and 
submissions from most of the associations of telecom service providers, several law firms and 
some public sector entiti es were received and all of them were considered and the rules were 
framed accordingly. While making submissions on the rule -wise features , it was submitted 
that t hese Rules establish a robust legal and operational framework for telecom security, 
ensuring compliance, accountability, and resilience against emerging cyber threats. 
2.3 In the submissions, t he interconnected nature of both rules was pointed out and the 
need for proactive measures to address the rapid advancements in technology and 
cybersecurity was emphasized. Issues relating to inter -ministerial coordination, particularly 
between the Department of Telecommunications (DoT), Ministry of Electronics and 
Information Technology (MeitY), Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA), and other relevant 
departments, to ensure effective collaboration in enforcing these rules were also mentioned. 
Points regarding the security of smart  phones and apps, particularly those manufactured in 
other countries and also about the testing and enforcement mechanism to ensure that devices 
entering the Indian market are free from malware or spyware  were also deliberated upon. 
Members of the Committee, raised concerns about cybercrime awareness, particularly in rural 
areas, and suggested leveraging government platforms like UPI, Aadhaar, and banking portals 
to disseminate cybersecurity awareness messages.  Queries also touched upon the need for 
better coordination with state governments and cyber police, particularly in addressing 
financial frauds targeting vulnerable groups like senior citizens.   
2.4 In summary, Secretary of the Department of Telecommunications (DoT), on the 
Telecom Cyber Security Rules  pointed out that they s erve as an overarch ing framework for 
telecom cyber security, covering telecom service providers and users misus ing telecom 
resources (e.g., for digital arrests or fraud)  and the Critical Telecommunication Infrastructure 
(CTI) Rules  enable the government to designate specific telecom infrastructure as critical, 
based on its impact on national security, economy, publ ic health, and safety.  In the Global 
context, this a ligns with international practices for protecting critical assets.  Also, it was 
emphasized that unlike the IT Act’s broader framework, CTI Rules are telecom-specific,  
7 

covering security standards, upgrades, and inspections  and facilitate a shift from the IT Act’  
critical information infrastructure framework to a telecom-focused one. 
2.5 While clarifying some queries by Members, Secretary outlined robust inter -ministerial 
coordination through the Digital Communications Commission (DCC), involving MeitY, 
NITI Aayog, Department of Economic Affairs(DEA) , Department for Promotion of Industry 
and Internal Trade ( DPIIT) , and collaboration with MHA’s Indian Cybercrime Coordination 
Centre (I4C),  the Ministry of Consumer Affairs, and Ministry of Micro, Small and Medium 
Enterprises( MSME) for cybercrime, unsolicited calls, and Industry 4.0. He stated that DoT 
coordinates with State Governments via Digital Intelligence Units and manages sp ectrum for 
law enforcement. The I4C portal facilitates cybercrime reporting with state police integration. 
On the Data Protection (DPDP) Rules, it was submitted that DoT is aligning telecom

Saathi’ app which empowers users to report fraudulent calls, block numbers, and reduce

2.6 During the meeting of the Committee on 11 th March, the Committee heard the 
submissions of the Telecommunication Engineering Centre (TEC) and National Centre for 
Communication Security (NCCS) on the matter.  
2.7 In their submissions, Secretary and Senior Officials of the Telecommunication 
Engineering Centre (TEC) stated that TEC serves as the technical arm of the Department of 
Telecommunications (DoT), acting as a knowledge hub and advis ory body for the telecom 
and ICT sectors. Its key functions include standardization, testing, and certification of 
telecommunication equipment, along with administration of the Mandatory Testing and 
Certification of Telecommunication Equipment (MTCTE) unde r the Indian Telegraph 
(Amendment) Rules, 2017and  Telecommunications (Standards, Conformity Assessment and 
Certification) Rules, 2025. It was mentioned that  TEC plays a crucial role in formulating 
technical standards, conducting field trials, and ensuring conformity assessment through 
various certification schemes like Type Approval Certificate (TAC), Interface Approval 
Certificate (IAC), Simplified Certification Scheme (SCS), and General Certification Scheme 
(GCS). Also, the MTCTE framework mandates equipm ent testing at TEC -designated labs, 
with an end -to-end online certification process. Additionally, TEC collaborates with global 
standardization bodies like ITU -T, ETSI, 3GPP, and ANSI , ensuring alignment with 
international best practices.

It was conveye d that the Government has also exempted specific telecom products such as

chips/Components/OS from land Border Countries, by third party/random inspections, need to 
use and prescribe Indian Operating Software including Mobile SIM Operating System, need 
to incorporate/mandate of Zero Trust Architecture; need to enhance incident response and 
recovery plans; need to encourage threat intelligence sharing platform; need to strengthen 
Supply Chain Security; need for Cybersecurity awareness and training; and need to establish a 
Cybersecurity Certification Framework.  He also highlighted some specific issues with rules 
provisions under the Teleco m Cyber Security Rules, 2024 before the Committee and suggest 
to include Virtual Telecom Network providers also in the definition under the Rules 2(f) and 
Rules 4(2) (b) need to define fraudulent messages; Rule 6 need to prescribe 
qualification/criteria for the role of CTSO etc. 
2.15 TEMA’s submissions also highlighted the importance of regular capability maturity 
assessments for Security Operation Centres and continuous professional development for 
cybersecurity personnel. They proposed the implementation of a National Firewall and 
monitoring only metadata at gateways to strengthen security.  
11 

Additionally, TEMA resubmitted Annexure 1 with clarifications and additional information, 
while Annexure 2 remained unchanged. Further submissions covered critical areas such as 
"Rip and Replacement" of vulnerable infrastructure, addressing white -labelling issues, 
leveraging Indian opportunities arising from U.S. tariff policies, and strategies to promote 
Indian standards globally. These recommendations aim to fortify India’s telecom 
cybersecurity framework and enhance its global competitiveness. 
3. Besides the oral submissions during the meetings of the Committee, the Department of 
Telecom in its written submissions , while responding to the Questionnaires sent in respect of 
the examination of Rules has provided information which is summarized as under:  
3.1 Submissions in respect of Critical Telecom Infrastructure (CTI) Rules, 2024: The 
Telecommunication Act, 2023 (Chapter IV, Sections 19–23) provides the legal foundation for 
standards, public safety, national security, and telecom network protection. Sectio n 22 
outlines CTI identification and security implementation. The CTI Rules include features 
beyond NCIIPC’s CII rules under the IT Act, such as mandatory compliance with telecom -
specific standards, log preservation for two years, risk registers, remote ac cess protocols, 
supply chain upgrade procedures, and a digital compliance framework.  Rule 9 of the CTI 
Rules directs punishment under the Telecommunication Act. Section 42(1) prescribes up to 
three years imprisonment or a ₹2 crore fine, or both, for unauth orized services or damaging 
CTI. Additional penalties apply under Sections 32 and 34 for authorization breaches. The 
Rules require that Service providers must submit detailed information on CTI components. 
These are reviewed for compliance with applicable security standards by the Telecom 
Engineering Centre (TEC) and the National Centre for Communication Security (NCCS).  The 
submissions mention that t he National Security Directive on Telecommunication Sector 
(effective since June 2021) mandates sourcing tel ecom equipment from trusted sources. 
National Security Council Secretariat (NSCS) manages this through the Trusted Telecom 
Portal, evaluating and approving equipment before deployment. Field inspections by DoT 
verify compliance.  DoT conducts annual inspections using updated proformas. CTI 
inspections will be integrated into this routine. Security incidents must be reported within six 
hours via email and later through a digital portal, as per Rule 7(1)(j) of the CTI Rules and 
definitions from the Telecom Cyber Security Rules, 2024.  Also, each service provider must 
designate a CTSO to oversee network security and compliance  whose responsibilities include 
maintaining architecture, access authorizations, risk analysis, incident reports , audits, SLAs, 
and updates to a centralized portal.TEC and NCCS formulate security standards in 
consultation with academic institutions like IITs which are published after stakeholder review.  
 
12 

Service providers are obligated to comply, with field insp ections ensuring adherence.  Also, 
entities must apply to DoT for planned upgrades. In urgent cases post -security incidents, 
immediate upgrades are permitted with post -facto intimation to DoT within 24 hours. All 
requests and reports will eventually be routed through a dedicated portal. 
3.2 Further submissions outline the framework for identifying and regulating telecom 
infrastructure critical to national security, public safety, and economic stability. A designated 
Committee within the Department of Telecommunications (DoT), including NCIIPC 
representatives, evaluates telecom networks to classify Critical Telecom Infrastructure (CTI) 
based on impact assessments. The MTCTE (Mandatory Testing and Certification of 
Telecommunication Equipment) framework is used for testing and certifying imported 
telecom hardware and software, with standards and test labs already established for various 
equipment categories. The  CTI Rules provide mechanisms for inspection, compliance, 
penalties, and data access with checks to safeguard privacy and prevent misuse. Inspections 
require prior notice to telecom entities, and a Chief Telecom Security Officer (CTSO) must be 
appointed by each entity to ensure rule implementation. Data access is res tricted to 
cybersecurity-related information, not personal data. The rules mandate incident reporting 
within six hours, with further detailed reporting timelines to be reviewed later. While prior 
government permission is required for CTI upgradation, excep tions are made for urgent 
security responses, and a 14 -day deemed approval process is included to reduce compliance 
delays. 
3.3 Submissions in respect of Telecom Cyber Security Rules, 2024 : The submissions 
outline a comprehensive framework for enhancing cy bersecurity in India’s telecom sector. 
The rules emphasize a "digital by design" approach, with Rule 10 mandating a dedicated 
portal for compliance and data submissions is currently under development by the Department 
of Telecommunications (DoT). Until the  portal is operational, interim measures like email -
based incident reporting aligned with CERT -IN timelines and existing license conditions for 
security policies are in place. The Ministry submits that the broad definitions in the rules  take 
into account the evolving nature of cyber threats and referenc e the IT Act, 2000, IT Rules, 
2009, and ITU standards to ensure inclusivity. Data confidentiality is prioritized through 
secure MPLS networks or VPNs, role -based access, and metadata -only collection 
(approximately 1% of traffic), with secure data centers restricting unauthorized access. 
3.4 Key operational aspects include mandatory Security Operations Centres (SOCs) for all 
telecom entities, as per Rule 4(4)( h), tasked with threat monitoring, logging, and supporting 
investigations. The ICDR portal facilitates IMEI registration, with Rules 8(4) and 8(5)  
13 

enabling the identification and removal of tampered IMEI devices without user hearings, 
following GSMA st andards. The Ministry acknowledges implementation challenges, such as 
portal development timelines and stakeholder training, but ensures safeguards like password -
protected, role -based access and contemporary security standards. Punitive measures under 
Rule 9 and Section 42 of the Act impose strict penalties for offences like fraudulent SIM 
procurement or tampering, with up to three years imprisonment or a ₹50 lakh fine. The 
Ministry also notes that no stakeholder objections have been received, indicating in itial 
acceptance of the rules. 
3.5 The Ministry’s responses to specific concerns address stakeholder feedback on 
ambiguities and implementation. For instance, the broad language in phrases like  “adequate 
safeguards” and “as may be specified” is justified as necessary for flexibility in the fast -
evolving telecom and cyber threat landscape, allowing for future adjustments. Rule 5 balances 
urgent suspension powers with a seven -day notice and 30 -day appeal mechanism for non -
urgent cases, ensuring grievance redressal. Data collection is limited to traffic data for 
cybersecurity purposes, with safeguards to prevent unauthorized access, and the Central 
Government may impose additional measures. The Mini stry acknowledges AI -driven cyber 
threats, noting that the rules are designed to accommodate emerging technologies and can be 
updated as needed. 
3.6 Further submissions state that the Rules f ortify India’s telecom infrastructure through 
digital compliance, robust security measures, and proactive threat management.  Through the 
development of the compliance portal, ongoing stakeholder training, and alignment with 
international standards like GSMA and ITU , the rules’ forward -looking approach has been 
underscored.  
3.7 The Ministry emphasizes that telecom cyber security is a rapidly evolving field, and 
thus, broader definitions and flexible mechanisms were intentionally designed to 
accommodate emerging threats and technological changes. Safeguards like password 
protection, role -based access, and adherence to future government -issued measures are 
mentioned, stating that many specifics will figure in the digital portal currently under 
development is operational.
